transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-05-18
Start: 16:30 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam Patel (Redwood SE), Sofia Alvarez (Redwood CSM), Jordan Reyes (CTO - Borealis), Priya Nair (Platform Eng), Ethan Cole (Data Eng), Samira Khan (Security Lead)
Links referenced: Redwood security packet (https://redwood.example/security-pack), sample SDK repo (https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk-samples), benchmark sheet (to be shared)

[00:00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call — can you hear me?
[00:00:06] Jordan (Borealis): Yep, loud and clear. Jordan here.
[00:00:08] Priya (Platform): Priya on my end.
[00:00:10] Ethan (Data): Ethan, hello.
[00:00:12] Samira (Security): Samira, security.
[00:00:15] Maya: Great, thanks. The plan for today is a broad integration discovery — SDKs, gateway patterns, quotas, and observability. We'll surface any hard constraints for you to evaluate Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private. Liam, do you want to kick into the runtime stuff?
[00:00:30] Liam (Redwood SE): Sure. Hi all — I'm Liam. I'll give a quick overview of how the serving runtime behaves and then we'll map that to your architecture questions. At a high level, Redwood supports our hosted API, reserved Dedicated pools, and a Private deployment for VPC/on-prem. Our SDKs are in JS, Python, and Go; we also provide LangChain and LlamaIndex adapters — sometimes the transcriber munges LlamaIndex as 'Lama index' — but yes, we have adapter layers.
[00:00:55] Jordan: Quick question — what's the difference for us between Dedicated and Private? If we need VPC and KMS, is Dedicated sufficient?
[00:01:05] Liam: Good q. Dedicated is a reserved GPU pool that's still in Redwood-managed infra but offers isolation and committed capacity. It supports VPC peering and private network paths but keys are by default managed via Redwood KMS unless you configure a customer-managed key. Private means the control plane can be customer-hosted or we deploy the entire stack inside customer VPC/on-prem — full data plane and control plane isolation, with options for HSM integrations.
[00:01:30] Priya: So Dedicated can do VPC peering but the control plane stays with you — that's the sticking point for compliance. Samira, is that acceptable?
[00:01:38] Samira: For some of our customers no, we need an auditable control plane and separate key ownership. SOC2 is table stakes. If you can do customer-managed key and audit logs being pushed to our SIEM that's okay but control plane egress is a blocker for certain regulated workloads.
[00:01:55] Maya: Understood. We'll share the SOC2 pack and the KMS/HSM options we support. Link will be in the deck.
[00:02:02] [00:02:02] Jordan: On the integration side, we run a microservices platform on Kubernetes, and we sit behind an internal API gateway (Kong/Envoy). Our main pattern is to put a sidecar for heavy inference-adjacent services — what's your recommended gateway/proxy pattern? Sidecar vs central gateway?
[00:02:20] Liam: We see both. For per-request low-latency it's common to use a local sidecar or agent that holds a persistent connection to the Redwood runtime (especially for KV cache reuse). That reduces round trips. Alternately a central gateway works for simpler routing but you pay extra egress and added tail latency — it can be fine for async or batch flows. If you need strict per-tenant rate quotas at the route level, a central gateway gives a single place to enforce it, but sidecars can also call a central rate service or use local leaky-bucket with periodic coordination.
[00:02:55] Priya: Interesting — our latency SLO for chat is 200ms P95, so sidecar seems appealing. But cost is a concern. How does caching interact with your Hosted offering? If we use Hosted, can we still get the KV cache locality we want?
[00:03:10] Liam: There's tradeoffs. Hosted supports prefix and KV caching at the service edge. For high locality and microsecond access you'd want the cache co-located — which typically implies Dedicated or Private. Hosted still does cache hits for repeated conversational flows, but if you have many shards and small hot sets, Dedicated with a pinned cache is more predictable. Also batching behavior in Hosted can affect tail latency as it optimizes throughput.
[00:03:32] [00:03:32] Jordan: That leads to the cost/latency question — do you provide tooling to simulate token-level costs per workload? We have a lot of short chat bursts and some long-document summarization jobs.
[00:03:42] Maya: Yes — Redwood Optimize recommendations give you quantization and batching suggestions, and we provide sample calculators. Liam can run a benchmark against your sample prompt corpus; that'll show per-token cost and latency projections for Hosted vs Dedicated.
[00:03:56] Liam: We'll also want your traffic histograms — tokens/response length, concurrency, and model choices. Even simple things like truncation or system prompt templating change the economics a lot.
[00:04:10] Ethan: We'll share a histogram. For LLM model choice — we plan to use a mixture of open models and some finetuned variants. How heavy is the SDK work to plug in LangChain and LlamaIndex?
[00:04:20] Liam: The SDKs are straightforward. Our LangChain connector is basically a chain wrapper; for LlamaIndex we have a storage-backed adapter that supports document embeddings and retrieval. Common gotcha: vector store connectors sometimes need batching alignment (embedding batch sizes), and you'll want to ensure consistency of embedding model versions between Redwood embedding endpoints and your vector index. We have sample notebooks for that.
[00:04:42] Priya: Do you provide rate limiting primitives at the route level? We need per-customer quotas and burst caps, with soft and hard limits.
[00:04:50] Maya: Yes, per-route and per-API-key quotas. You can set token-based quotas, request-per-minute, and burst windows. There's also a policy engine for graceful degradation — e.g., fallback to a smaller model variant or queuing when limits are hit.
[00:05:05] Samira: How are rate-limit violations surfaced? We need audit logs and traces for any dropped requests.
[00:05:10] Liam: Violations emit structured events to the observability pipeline; they appear in the Console's event timeline and can be exported to your SIEM or to Datadog via our logging hooks. We also attach request_id and correlation_id so you can tie it to traces.
[00:05:20] [00:05:20] Jordan: Observability — we use Datadog + OpenTelemetry. Do you accept OTLP?
[00:05:25] Liam: Yes, we can forward OTLP traces. We also support exporting Prometheus metrics, and we have a Datadog integration that maps Redwood tokens, latency, and cost per route. Note that sampling strategies are configurable to avoid bill shock on high-volume debug traces.
[00:05:40] Priya: Do you provide SDK hooks to attach our tracing spans or do we need to instrument upstream?
[00:05:44] Liam: SDKs include wrappers to propagate trace context (W3C traceparent) and to annotate token counts per span. For some customers we suggest instrumenting at the gateway layer so you get consistent correlation across non-LLM services.
[00:05:58] Ethan: What's the deployment/upgrade path for Private? We anticipate quarterly model rollout windows and want canarying capabilities.
[00:06:05] Liam: Private supports the same rollout primitives as Hosted — canary, A/B, and automatic fallback. For on-prem we provide Helm charts and a deployment operator; rollouts are controlled via the control plane which can be run in your VPC in the Private model. Canary traffic can be routed by percent or by header.
[00:06:20] Jordan: Pricing and procurement — any flexibility on committed throughput pricing if we commit to a year?
[00:06:25] Maya: Yes, Dedicated reserved capacity comes with committed monthly throughput and discounts, and enterprise Private deals are contract-negotiated. We'll do a Dedicated vs Private pricing review in the next meeting with procurement.
[00:06:35] Samira: On security, we need to know where logs live and retention controls. Also SSO (SAML) and RBAC for our engineers.
[00:06:42] Maya: SSO via SAML is supported, RBAC with teams and roles is in Console. Log retention is configurable for Dedicated and Private; Hosted has retention tiers. We'll include retention tables in the security packet.
[00:06:55] [00:06:55] Priya: A couple of nitty-gritty questions — 1) do you expose per-request token accounting in the response headers? 2) Is there an idempotency token semantics for retries?
[00:07:05] Liam: 1) Yes, you can request token and prompt/completion breakdowns in headers. 2) We support idempotency keys for non-streaming calls; streaming has at-least-once semantics, so we provide sequence tokens to help you deduplicate if you implement a client-side buffer.
[00:07:20] Ethan: For streaming, how does reconnect and partial resume work? We need to resume mid-stream on flaky mobile networks.
[00:07:25] Liam: We support streaming with delta-chunks and a resumable token — it's not perfect for every mobile case, but for reconnections we provide a resume token that encodes the conversation offset and KV cache pointer, which reduces re-generation. There are edge cases with model internal state; we'll detail them in an engineering note.
[00:07:45] Jordan: Any limits on model sizes for Dedicated vs Hosted? For example can we bring a 70B finetuned model to Dedicated?
[00:07:52] Liam: Dedicated supports large models up to the hardware the pool contains; we can provision GPU types per customer roadmaps. Private on-prem obviously depends on your hardware. For very large model hosting we recommend Dedicated with instance types that match memory/compute needs. We'll need to validate your specific model size and quantization plan.
[00:08:10] [00:08:10] Priya: Integration example — we currently call OpenAI directly from our gateway. If we move to Redwood, we want a drop-in proxy that preserves headers and SSO context. Is there an easy proxy shim?
[00:08:20] Maya: We have a small gateway shim and an OpenAPI-compatible proxy mode. You can route existing traffic to Redwood endpoints with minimal code changes, and our shim preserves headers and forwards auth into the Redwood API keys or SAML-backed tokens.
[00:08:34] Samira: How do you handle data residency? We have EU customers.
[00:08:38] Liam: We have region-aware routing and can pin models/data to EU-only regions for Dedicated and Private. Hosted has regional endpoints as well, but if you need strict legal control, Private is the strongest guarantee.
[00:08:50] Jordan: Let's talk quotas again — if a tenant exceeds quota, do you throttle or reject? Can we tier traffic?
[00:08:56] Liam: Both. You can configure soft throttles (queueing with exponential backoff), and hard rejections with 429. There are also policy actions like fallback to a cheaper model or returning cached responses.
[00:09:07] [00:09:07] Priya: For billing granularity, do you support per-tenant metering in Dedicated? We want to charge internal teams.
[00:09:13] Maya: Yes, token-level metering by API-key or tenant-id is supported and exports to billing reports in Console. For Dedicated we can also push usage records to your billing system via webhook.
[00:09:25] Ethan: Sample bench — can you run variance across concurrency? Our 95th percentile is sensitive to concurrent spikes.
[00:09:30] Liam: Absolutely. For the benchmark we'll simulate your concurrency pattern and show P50/P95/P99 for token latency, and cost per 1k tokens. We'll include KV cache hit-rate assumptions.
[00:09:42] Jordan: Any known gotchas with LangChain connectors and async chains? We use async orchestration heavily.
[00:09:48] Liam: LangChain async is supported in our Python SDK; you just need to ensure the event loop is not blocked by synchronous SDK calls. The other gotcha is stream handling and callback managers — we provide async-friendly callback handlers.
[00:10:00] Maya: Quick pause — does anyone have burning questions before we move into a short architecture sketch from Priya's notes?
[00:10:06] Priya: No, go ahead.
[00:10:08] [00:10:08] Priya (reading architecture): So we have a Kubernetes mesh with Envoy fronting services. We plan to place a small Redwood sidecar as an envoy filter on the nodes that host chat frontends. The sidecar will maintain persistent connections for low latency and also hold a local small cache for hot prompts. For long docs we'll route to a central summarization service. Concerns: token accounting coherence and rate-limiting enforcement across sidecars.
[00:10:35] Liam: That pattern maps well to our recommendations. For token coherency we usually centralize quota enforcement via a token-service that sidecars consult with short TTLs, or we opt-in for distributed counters with eventual reconciliation depending on strictness required.
[00:10:50] Samira: From a security POV, if sidecars have long-lived credentials they become a token target. Do you support short-lived creds with mTLS?
[00:10:57] Liam: Yes — mTLS is supported for private link connections and we strongly recommend short-lived tokens via our Vault integration or via your KMS + short-lived certs.
[00:11:08] Jordan: What about observability at the token level — can we trace a user conversation across multiple services into Redwood logs?
[00:11:15] Liam: Yes, with correlation ids and OpenTelemetry propagation you can stitch everything together — the Console also exposes a conversation timeline that includes token counts, model used, and cache hits.
[00:11:25] [00:11:25] Maya: We're about a third of the way through — saving the heavy technical follow-up for Liam and Priya to coordinate. Quick commercial question — do you have an expected timeline to decision?
[00:11:33] Jordan: We're aiming for a pilot in June and then a Q3 production ramp, but procurement and security need to sign off by mid-June. So tight.
[00:11:41] Maya: Noted — we'll prioritize SOC2/KMS docs and a benchmark deck first.
[00:11:47] [00:11:47] Priya: A couple of specific feature asks — 1) ability to pin a fallback model by route, 2) per-tenant warmup quotas to avoid cold start spikes. Are those available?
[00:11:57] Liam: Both supported. Fallback policies are route-configurable. Warmup quotas we implement via gradual ramp policies and pre-warming kernels to avoid cold starts; we'll add an implementation note for your ops team.
[00:12:10] Ethan: Any restrictions on embedding model versions for LlamaIndex? If we switch embedding models we may need to reindex. Do you support versioned embedding endpoints so we can maintain backward compatibility?
[00:12:19] Liam: We do support versioned embedding endpoints; it's a good practice to namespace embedding models in your vector store to avoid reindexing unless you want to. We'll include embedding strategy notes.
[00:12:30] [00:12:30] Jordan: Can you talk about failure modes? If a Dedicated pool has a hardware outage, what's the fallback?
[00:12:36] Liam: We have multi-pool failover and can auto-fallback to smaller models in a different region, or to Hosted as a last resort. For mission-critical customers we recommend cross-region Dedicated pools or Private with active/standby. Failovers are surfaced in Console and can be set to auto-route.
[00:12:52] Samira: Are failover events logged in a way that's auditable for compliance?
[00:12:55] Maya: Yes — all failovers and routing changes are in the audit log with timestamps and actor metadata.
[00:13:02] [00:13:02] Priya: Let's talk minimal POC — what would you recommend?
[00:13:06] Liam: A small pilot: 1) run a benchmark using your top 20 prompts, 2) deploy sidecar on a staging node for chat flows, 3) validate KV cache hit-rate and latency over 48 hours, 4) run security review with Samira and confirm key management. That should be 2-3 weeks.
[00:13:23] Jordan: Sounds good. If we do the pilot on Hosted first to iterate quickly, can we port to Dedicated with the same config?
[00:13:29] Liam: Porting is designed to be seamless: same API, model naming, and rollout semantics. There are infra-specific knobs (cache placement, kernel selection) that you'll tune when moving to Dedicated.
[00:13:41] [00:13:41] Maya: Ok let's capture next steps — I'll send SOC2 + KMS + SSO docs, Liam will run the benchmark and share a result sheet, Priya will send traffic histograms, and we'll meet again for pricing. Any objections?
[00:13:56] Priya: No objections.
[00:13:58] Jordan: All good.
[00:14:00] [00:14:00] Samira: One more Q — SLA expectations for Dedicated?
[00:14:04] Maya: Dedicated has SLA-backed uptime and latency targets; we'll include the SLA PDF in the packet. Private SLAs are contract-negotiated.
[00:14:12] Ethan: A note about SDKs — our stack is mostly Node + Python. Any code samples we should look at for the sidecar integration?
[00:14:19] Liam: We'll share Node and Python sidecar examples in the sample repo. The Node example shows envoy filter integration and token propagation.
[00:14:28] [00:14:28] Jordan: Timeline recap — SOC2 + benchmark by next Wed, pricing review next week, pilot in June.
[00:14:36] Maya: Yep. Any additional blockers?
[00:14:39] Priya: Not at this time.
[00:14:40] [00:14:40] Maya: Great — we'll send meeting notes and action items. Thanks everyone.
[00:14:45] Jordan: Thanks.
[00:14:46] Priya: Thanks all.
[00:14:47] Ethan: Thanks.
[00:14:48] Samira: Thanks.
